name: Salus: Fine-Grained GPU Sharing Primitives for Deep Learning Applications
problem: GPUs lack fine-grained sharing primitives, so time-sharing and preemption between DL applications are expensive, and when one application cannot fill a GPU the device is wasted for everyone else.
mechanism: Build fine-grained sharing from unmodified GPUs by interleaving kernels from concurrent applications at a granularity the stock scheduler already supports, with a monitor that decides when to interleave so each application still sees useful progress.
speedup_reported: NOT RECORDED as a multiple — the arXiv abstract describes fine-grained GPU sharing primitives without a verified headline number carrying baseline and settings. Also note the scope mismatch: these are DL training/application-sharing results on V100-era GPUs, predating both MIG and LLM inference serving. Read the paper for the utilisation and fairness comparison against whole-GPU time sharing.
notes:
VENUE NOT VERIFIED — the arXiv comment is empty, USENIX site search returns no Salus paper, and ACM DL is antibot-blocked, so I record arxiv-preprint rather than guess EuroSys. Adoption 'abandoned' is a deliberate, evidence-based call: the software-sharing approach was superseded by hardware partitioning (NVIDIA MIG) and by CUDA MPS, which is the mechanism NVIDIA actually ships for GPU sharing today. Salus remains a well-cited systems paper whose premise the industry solved a different way.
